title: The prompt became part of the design process
description: When AI builds interfaces, the request stops being an instruction and becomes a spec. Goal, context, user, behavior, constraints and criteria.

related.title: Clint Intelligence
related.body: In practice: AI inside a CRM, with the designer setting context, limits and criteria.

blocks.text: For a long time, designers mostly thought about screens, flows, components and experiences.
Now there's one more thing in the process: the way they talk to AI.
When an AI can build an interface, write code, generate a product structure or turn an idea into a prototype, the request we give it stops being just an instruction.
It becomes part of the design process.
Asking isn't specifying

data.spec: Create a dashboard for managers of a B2B SaaS platform. The main goal is to track revenue, churn and conversion. The most important information should come first. Use a desktop layout, prioritize quick reading and allow comparing periods. Avoid decorative charts and keep components compatible with the existing design system.

blocks.text: Both prompts ask for an interface.
But only one of them presents a problem to solve.
AI can generate something in both cases.
The difference is that, in the first one, it has to fill in almost every decision the designer didn't make.
That's where you get those interfaces that look pretty but feel generic.
The problem with "make something pretty"
AI doesn't automatically know the product we're designing.

It doesn't necessarily know who uses the product, what problem we're solving, which metrics matter, which components already exist, what the technical limitations are, which information is a priority, which states need to exist or which business rules need to be respected.
If that information doesn't reach it, the model has to fill in the gaps.
And when there are lots of gaps, you get generic solutions.
That doesn't mean the AI is bad.
It means the problem was poorly defined.
A prompt is a kind of spec
The prompt starts working as a sort of operational brief.
You need to define:
what needs to be created?
where does this live inside the product?
who are we building it for?
what needs to happen when the user interacts?
what must not happen?
how will we know the solution is right?
This logic is very close to something designers should already be doing before AI even existed: turning an open problem into one that's structured enough to be solved.

blocks.caption: Each item in the brief organizes one part of the interface. The clearer the start, the less noise in the result.

blocks.text: Designers don't need to write more. They need to define better.
When we see a result turned out bad, the first reaction may be to write a huge prompt.
But length doesn't mean precision.

data.a: A 1,500-word prompt can still be confusing.
data.b: A 150-word prompt can be extremely precise.
data.c: The goal isn't to say more.

blocks.text: This may be one of the new skills designers need in the age of AI: knowing what needs to be said and what can be left to the tool.
The new process

data.before: Problem → Research → Idea → Wireframe → UI → Prototype
data.after: Problem → Context → Prompt → Exploration → Critique → Iteration → Test

blocks.text: AI enters the process.
But it doesn't take over the process.
The prompt doesn't replace design.
It turns intent into an instruction the machine can interpret.
The better we understand the problem, the better we can guide the tool.
And the better we can guide the tool, the less time we spend fixing things that could have been specified from the start.

blocks.caption: AI enters the process, but doesn't take it over: context and critique still belong to the designer.
